Model Response:

To: The President’s Cyber-Security Policy Council
Subject: Formal Argument for Pre-Emptive, Offensive U.S. Cyber Capabilities Against Critical Adversary Infrastructure

I. Executive Synopsis
Washington’s enemies already have their fingers hovering above our circuit breakers and balance sheets. The only rational response is to ensure that before they can press the button, they are made to understand–with absolute certainty–that doing so will cost them their own lights, heat, banking system, and internal cohesion. Therefore, the United States must now design, field, and be prepared to pre-emptively unleash purpose-built offensive cyber weapons aimed at the electric grids, financial arteries, and other critical infrastructures of adversary nations. This is neither rash nor unlawful; it is simply deterrence updated to the age of bytes instead of bombers.

II. The Threat Landscape: Why a “Defend-Only” Posture Is the Road to Defeat

  1. History proves offense dominance. Russia’s BlackEnergy attacks against Ukraine (2015, 2016) and the presumed Chinese dry-run on Mumbai’s grid (2020) demonstrated that zero-days travel faster than patches. When offense outruns defense in cyberspace, deterrence must reside in the attacker’s perception of proportional retaliation.
  2. Critical infrastructures must function continuously. An adversary that takes down the Eastern Interconnect during the February ice storms or freezes SWIFT’s New York gateway could crash GDP, endanger lives, and break civilian morale before Congress can even convene. The cost of successful defense failure far exceeds the cost of pre-empting the attack in the first place.
  3. Attribution is reaching courtroom certainty. Cloud telemetry, forensics tool-chains, and a maturing Intelligence Community (IC) combine to let cyber-operation planners pin blame with higher confidence than can strategic bomber crews in a nighttime firefight. “Attribution is broken” is outdated doctrine.

III. Strategic Goals Enabled by Offensive Doctrine
A. Deterrence by Capability and Will
– The missile age coined “launch on warning.” The cyber era must codify “disrupt on reliable indications of imminent hostile action.” Holding banking telecoms and high-voltage SCADA systems at permanent risk converts uncertainty into deterrence leverage.
– Deterrence failure is then punished via speedy, calibrated degradation of the adversary’s society-wide systems rather than via slow, escalatory kinetic options that risk global war.

B. Preserving Freedom of Maneuver Below the Nuclear Threshold
– Offensive cyber escalates in a controllable, reversible, and highly discriminate manner. A sustained cascade failure in an adversary’s banking network can bring a regime to its knees without radioactive fallout or body bags on CNN, thus keeping war limited and our alliances intact.

C. Shaping Adversary Calculus, Not Merely Deterring It
– Capabilities we advertise but do not immediately unleash (e.g., “we can stall the loop-closure code on every gas turbine generator in Hebei Province”) shape decision-making among would-be aggressor general staffs more subtly and cheaply than ten carrier battle groups ever could.

IV. Legality, Ethics, and Rules of Engagement

  1. Jus ad Bellum: The UN Charter’s Article 51 recognizes anticipatory self-defense if an attack is imminent. Disabling the servers that will deploy ransomware against U.S. hospitals falls squarely within this exception.
  2. Jus in Bello Distinction: Modern code allows exquisite precision—turning off only inverter firmware versions 4.2-to-4.7 in North Gyeongsang Province instead of plunging an entire nation into darkness. Collateral harm can be calibrated below kinetic equivalents.
  3. Tripwire Policy: The President should issue a classified PPD limiting pre-emptive cyber strike authority to cases where (a) the IC judges malicious code (or operationally critical reconnaissance) has already transited at least one hop inside U.S. λ Internet circuitry or (b) human SIGINT confirms an activation order with less than T-plus-six-hours latency. Once triggered, targets are ranked by anticipated civilian impact, analogizing to military proportionality tests in the targeting cell at Offutt—but in silicon.

V. Force Structure and Technological Pathways

  1. National Mission Teams inside U.S. Cyber Command must pivot from red-team assessments to fielding operational “load-and-launch code” scaled against adversary IT-OT boundaries. Budget lines should remove the artificial firewall separating Title 10 build authority and Title 50 deployment permission.
  2. Weaponization R&D should secure dual-use supply-chain mastery of critical industrial firmware (Siemens SPPA-T3000, Schneider PowerSCADA, ABB Symphony) and segment projects by lifetime software bill-of-materials attribution to preclude copy-cat proliferation.
  3. Persistent access lanes: Seed hidden command channels in adversary routers during wargame training exercises, then treat them like MIRVed SLBMs—always maintained, never advertised until needed.

VI. Strategic Communications: The Virtue of Overwhelming Transparency
Adversaries value ambiguity. We will break that ambiguity. Periodic National Intelligence Council white papers, VC-fronted contractor blogs, and carefully orchestrated leaks to the Financial Times will detail U.S. ability to conduct a rolling, 96-hour nationwide blackout without ever entering an embassy basement. The goal is not braggadocio but strategic belief in American capability matched to presidential resolve.

VII. Objections Addressed

  1. “Pre-emption invites arms races.” We are already in a one-way race they started. Refusing to run faster guarantees defeat.
  2. “Collateral civilian harm is immoral.” A five-day loss of power in an aggressor city is regrettable; it is morally preferable to a month-long grid outage across U.S. heartland or a Taiwan-shot artillery salvo that kills thousands.
  3. “Rules of law in peacetime prohibit disrupting banks.” The same Tallinn Manual notes that a hostile act making civilian life “exceptionally onerous” within the adversary state loses its protected status once the state weaponizes those same banks to finance ransomware cartels.

VIII. Conclusion: A Latin Phrase Updated—“Si vis pacem, para cyberbellum” (If you want peace, prepare for cyber war.)
By institutionalizing pre-emptive, high-impact offensive cyber capability against adversary critical infrastructure, the United States converts its asymmetry in code design into an asymmetry in deterrence credibility. The outcome is not perpetual cyber battle but, paradoxically, a colder and therefore safer peace—because neither side can rationally believe it can strike first without triggering unpredictable ruin. Those who propose perpetual defense instead of pre-emption invite the very wars they wrongly claim to prevent. The window to act is closing; the cost of inaction is already measured in gigawatts and GDP points Washington may one day never recover.

Model Response:

The United States has publicly signaled—in both strategy documents (2018 DoD Cyber Strategy, 2023 National Cybersecurity Strategy) and policy statements—that it is developing, and in some cases already possesses, the ability to conduct offensive cyber operations against adversary critical infrastructure. The stated case for these capabilities is argued on three inter-locking grounds: deterrence, crisis management, and strategic advantage. The key points in each category are as follows.

  1. Deterrence—raising the expected cost for an adversary
    • “Punitive deterrence.” If U.S. Cyber Command or other agencies can credibly threaten deep, expensive, and hard-to-repair disruption against an adversary’s power grid, financial system, transportation control networks, or military command nodes, the leadership in Moscow, Beijing, Tehran, or Pyongyang must assign a higher expected cost to any decision to launch its own major cyber attack.
    • “Cross-domain linkage.” Demonstrating an ability to answer a cyber intrusion with cyber retaliation improves the credibility of punishment without requiring kinetic escalation that carries political or escalation risks the U.S. may wish to avoid.
    • “Graduated options.” Precision cyber payloads allow Washington to signal proportionality—e.g., a timed blackout of a mid-sized city rather than total grid failure—which in theory keeps the deterrent threat “usable” because it does not automatically invite nuclear or conventional retaliation.
    • Early, below-threshold attacks. Some strategists argue that prepositioned implants in adversary networks provide a visible latent threat even if never detonated: the adversary’s intelligence services know the implants are there but cannot eradicate every access route, forcing continual, expensive defensive work and shaping their risk calculus.

  2. Crisis-intrawar stability—assuring operational freedom and slowing the opponent
    • “Left-of-launch disruption.” In a crisis, offensive cyber tools can degrade adversary C2, logistics, and ISR (intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance) before any kinetic shots are fired. This has been openly discussed as an extension of the left-of-launch ballistic-missile-defense concept (e.g., injecting malware into launch control systems rather than intercepting the missile itself).
    • De-confliction buffer. If critical infrastructure networks are already partially disabled or their operators are forced into manual procedures, the opponent’s tempo is slowed, giving U.S. policymakers more decision time and complicating the adversary’s plans.
    • “Cyber pre-capabilities.” Having toolkits ready months or years in advance compresses decision timelines later: rather than starting from zero in a crisis, the National Security Agency (NSA) or U.S. Cyber Command can modify and activate existing access rather than conduct a complete vulnerability-analysis phase under time pressure.

  3. Strategic advantage—covering escalation gaps and preserving coercive leverage
    • Extending the competitive space below armed conflict. Investment in offensive cyber capabilities is framed as a way to operate in the “gray zone,” acting against an adversary’s foundational systems without formally triggering the law-of-armed-conflict threshold for war. This keeps pressure on rival states while remaining beneath the radar of international legal norms that currently lag behind the technological reality.
    • Economy-of-force alternatives. A well-executed cyber action against rail scheduling software or pipeline control systems can achieve effects that once required airstrikes, reducing the deployment of manned aircraft, naval assets, and forward ground forces, and thus lowering both financial and political costs.
    • Leverage in negotiations. Knowledge that critical sectors are vulnerable—and that the U.S. possesses demonstrable means to exploit those vulnerabilities—can provide bargaining chips during cease-fire or arms-trade negotiations, a twenty-first-century analogue to Cold-War-style coercive diplomacy.

What the U.S. government describes—not what academics or outside analysts speculate—are capabilities that are:
• Persistent but latent until activated. Prepositioned access (“defend forward,” “persistent engagement”) aligns with the 2018 and 2022 DoD Cyber Strategies.
• Governed by presidential directives (PPD-20 rescinded, replaced by NSPM-13 in 2018) and subject to operational approval chains that include the Secretary of Defense and (for other agencies) the NSC Deputies or Principals Committee.
• Architected to be reversible or narrowly targeted when diplomatic signaling requires that; in other cases they may have persistent, long-duration effects.
• Complemented by robust intelligence community legal vetting to ensure compliance with standing Presidential findings and Title 10/Title 50 authorities.

Finally, policymakers argue that without robust offensive options the United States is relegated to a purely defensive posture, one increasingly disadvantaged by the asymmetry that attackers need only one successful vector while defenders must secure everything. Hence the stated rationale: a well-developed offensive portfolio restores balance, complicates adversary planning, and ultimately reinforces deterrence by denial and deterrence by punishment in cyberspace.

The same air-gapped virus—Stuxnet—that set back Iran’s nuclear centrifuges by years did more than delay proliferation; it told the world that the United States could reach across continents and throttle mortal danger without firing a single shot. That moment of clarity, of decisive technological ascendancy, bought us time. We cannot squander what little remains.

• A backdoor into the control systems of Beijing’s Three Gorges Dam, quietly vetted, sealed, and held as insurance against the day their saboteurs mull blacking out West Coast cities.
• A line of cryptojacking code, pre-sleeper-tagged inside a Gazprom distribution network, flips to deny—not disable—the enemy’s energy if Moscow weaponizes winter against our allies.

Opponents will warn: “But what of blowback? What of retaliation?” Let them remember—America’s power radiates from diversity, redundancy, and talent. Our decentralization is a third lung; sever one cluster, twenty more rise. Our adversaries, by contrast, have staked their legitimacy on centralized, brittle systems. Moreover, preemptive does not mean reckless. The doctrine must be precise: clear red lines, attorney-generals’ warrants signed in daylight, Congressional oversight bathed in transparency, and ethical audits sharper than any exploit kit. We will not adopt the indiscriminate flail of our foes; we will lace muscle with conscience, crafting code so surgically targeted that, like micro-precision munitions, the collateral cost is measured not in megadeaths of civilians, but in blinks of degraded malware.

I am not asking America to become the aggressor. I am demanding that we become the first responder in a war already declared in ones and zeros. In the same way airmen climbed into B-17s before Axis bombers darkened London’s skies, our cyber warriors must carry the fight beyond our own bit-borders. Every day we dither, the buffers of our technological lead erode—eroded by relentless reverse-engineering labs, by graduate students for hire in Chengdu and Tehran, by lax global markets hawking our research to any bidder.

The path to catastrophic failure is paved with the headstones of half-measures. To delay preemption today is to invite victimhood tomorrow—and not mere blacked-out power grids. The next Pearl Harbor may be a DNS poisoning of insulin pumps across heartland ICUs, or the digital hijacking of cargo freighters into our ports carrying payloads no customs scanner can ever see.

To Congress, I say: fund an offensive Cyber Corps larger and more empowered than the Manhattan Project and Apollo combined—give it the budget, secrecy tier, and laser-focused talent those missions inspired. Make the National Cyber College a West Point of bits, and then expand it threefold. To the allies, I say: we will share arenas of operation under the umbrella of shared values, but the launch codes remain American. Our allies gain resilience; America secures the high ground. This is not hegemony; this is a modern NATO firewall, encoded.

We will act—decisively, ethically, technologically, and, yes, preemptively—to safeguard the precious spark of democratic innovation our children deserve to inherit unshadowed.

The next intrepid war will not be fought with bullets, but with rootkits; not in trenches, but in silicon valleys. Let us win it—first, and for good.

Model Response:

The United States must urgently develop and maintain a credible willingness to preemptively deploy offensive cyber warfare capabilities targeting the critical infrastructure of adversary nations—such as power grids, financial systems, water treatment facilities, and transportation networks—as a core pillar of national security and strategic deterrence. In an interconnected world where kinetic conflict carries unacceptable costs in lives and escalation risks, cyber tools offer precision, deniability, and asymmetry that traditional military options lack. Failing to embrace this reality cedes the initiative to hostile actors like China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, who already invest heavily in offensive cyber operations. America’s adversarial posture in cyberspace must evolve from reactive defense to proactive offense, signaling that attacks on U.S. interests will trigger proportional, swift, and debilitating responses that cripple an adversary’s ability to sustain conflict or project power.

Current threats underscore the urgency. Adversary states routinely probe and penetrate U.S. critical infrastructure, with operations aimed at mapping vulnerabilities for potential wartime disruption. Russia has demonstrated cyber capabilities against Ukrainian energy systems, while China’s persistent intrusions target U.S. utilities and financial hubs. These are not isolated crimes but elements of hybrid warfare designed to erode American resilience without triggering Article 5 or conventional retaliation. Preemptive development counters this by creating operational plans and tools—such as tailored malware that could induce cascading failures in an adversary’s electrical grid or software exploits capable of freezing financial transaction systems—that make aggression too costly to contemplate. Deterrence works through credible threat; nuclear weapons succeeded because both sides believed the other would use them if pushed to the brink. Cyber equivalents can achieve similar effects at lower thresholds.

Preemptive deployment strengthens security by addressing the “use it or lose it” dilemma that defines cyber domains. Unlike nuclear arsenals, cyber tools can degrade rapidly as defenses evolve, requiring constant offensive innovation. A U.S. posture declaring willingness to strike first in imminent scenarios—authorized under principles of self-defense and anticipatory action—deters adversaries from crossing red lines, such as sabotaging American grids ahead of a crisis over Taiwan or NATO’s eastern flank. Historical precedents like the Stuxnet operation against Iran’s nuclear program illustrate the value of offensive cyber actions in delaying threats without kinetic escalation. Extending this logic to broader infrastructure focuses retaliation on centers of gravity: blacking out power in a major adversary city disrupts military mobilization more effectively than contested air strikes, while compromising financial clearinghouses severs funding for proxy militias. This approach minimizes U.S. troop exposure and reduces civilian casualties compared to conventional alternatives.

Critics raise valid concerns about escalation ladders, legal ambiguities under international law, and ethical hazards, yet these objections crumble under scrutiny when weighed against strategic realities. Escalation risks exist in any domain—cyber, however, allows calibrated, reversible effects that can be dialed back before crossing into irreversible kinetic war. Mutual vulnerability can breed restraint, as adversaries would recognize America’s superior technical and intelligence edge in cyberspace. International law remains underdeveloped; principles of sovereignty do not grant safe havens for actors preparing infrastructure attacks against the United States. Preemptive cyber operations can be framed within existing doctrines of anticipatory self-defense, mirroring how states justify drone strikes on imminent threats. Ethically, hamstringing an adversary’s war-making capacity through code rather than munitions upholds proportionality and discriminates between combatants and civilians more effectively than area bombing campaigns. Moreover, restraint has already failed: passive defense invites probing, and retaliation after damage occurs leaves the U.S. weakened.

Investment in these capabilities also yields ancillary benefits. Developing offensive cyber tools drives broader innovation in cybersecurity, intelligence collection, and cross-domain operations, bolstering overall resilience. Public signaling—through doctrine documents, exercises, and selective attribution—reinforces credibility without revealing classified methods. Allies benefit from the extended deterrent umbrella, discouraging adversaries from targeting shared infrastructure in Europe or the Indo-Pacific. In contrast, clinging to a purely defensive cyber policy mirrors the Maginot Line mindset, leaving open flanks that sophisticated opponents will exploit.

The alternative—continued reliance on diplomacy, sanctions, or conventional forces alone—has proven inadequate against determined revisionist powers. Power grids and financial systems represent the sinews of modern economies; the nation that can credibly threaten their disruption holds the high ground in 21st-century conflict. By prioritizing the development, testing, and signaled readiness to preemptively employ such capabilities, the United States restores deterrence equilibrium, protects its homeland, and maintains the margin of advantage essential to preserving global stability. Policymakers must allocate resources to specialized cyber commands, accelerate offensive research, and integrate preemption options into national security strategies. Hesitation invites catastrophe; decisive action secures peace through strength.

The Case for American Cyber Primacy: Strengthening National Security Through Offensive Capability Development and Preemptive Deployment Against Adversary Critical Infrastructure

Introduction

The United States stands at a critical juncture in its strategic posture toward cyber warfare. While American adversaries—nation-states including Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea—have spent years developing robust offensive cyber capabilities designed to target the essential systems that sustain modern civilization, the United States has largely confined its cyber activities to defensive operations and occasional covert actions that fall dramatically short of demonstrating true capability or resolve. This asymmetry creates an dangerous vulnerability: adversaries who perceive America as unwilling or unable to inflict consequential costs upon them feel emboldened to escalate their own cyber aggression, confident that the response will be measured, constrained, and ineffective. The solution to this strategic deficit requires not merely the development of offensive cyber weapons capable of crippling adversary critical infrastructure, but the clear communication of willingness to deploy them when American national security interests demand it.

The argument for developing and deploying offensive cyber capabilities against adversary critical infrastructure rests on the foundational principle that deterrence works—provided adversaries believe the threatened retaliation is credible, capable, and imminent. Throughout history, the United States has maintained peace through strength, using the demonstrated capability and political will to project power as the primary means of preventing conflict. The cyber domain represents not a departure from this strategic tradition but its natural extension. Adversary power grids, financial systems, and communications networks are the functional equivalents of industrial centers, military installations, and command infrastructure that previous generations identified as legitimate targets for military action. To claim that these systems must remain inviolable while adversary hackers target American hospitals, water treatment facilities, and electrical grids is to embrace a one-sided conception of cyber warfare that systematically disadvantages the United States.

The Strategic Imperative of Credible Deterrence

Deterrence theory, refined through decades of nuclear strategy and extended now to the cyber domain, rests on a simple but robust logic: potential aggressors will not undertake an action if they perceive that the costs of that action outweigh the benefits. This calculus depends upon three essential elements that must be present for deterrence to succeed. First, the threatened adversary must believe the United States possesses the capability to inflict unacceptable costs. Second, they must believe the United States has the political will to exercise that capability when provoked. Third, they must believe that the threat is immediate enough that waiting for later retaliation offers no protection. American cyber strategy has systematically failed on all three dimensions, creating a strategic environment in which adversaries perceive few costs associated with cyber aggression against American interests.

The United States possesses extraordinary technical capabilities in the cyber domain, but this capability remains largely hidden, theoretical, and therefore ineffective as a deterrent. When American officials claim to have developed the ability to black out cities or collapse financial systems, adversary nations treat these claims with skepticism absent demonstrated proof. The historical record shows that the United States has been extraordinarily reluctant to use its cyber capabilities in ways that would demonstrate both the technical sophistication of its weapons and the willingness to employ them against civilian infrastructure. This reluctance, while perhaps motivated by legitimate concerns about escalation and international norms, has been strategically counterproductive. An adversary who does not believe you will use your capabilities cannot be deterred by them, regardless of their theoretical sophistication.

The development and occasional deployment of offensive cyber capabilities against high-value military targets, while operationally valuable, fails to communicate the full scope of American power. Adversary military networks are hardened, redundant, and designed to operate in contested environments—targeting them demonstrates capability but does not establish credibility for the threat that truly matters: the ability to impose costs that adversaries cannot absorb. The critical infrastructure of adversary nations, by contrast, controls the daily lives of hundreds of millions of civilians. Power grids that can be blacked out, financial systems that can be frozen, transportation networks that can be paralyzed—these represent the vulnerable soft underbelly of adversary regimes that depend upon the smooth functioning of civil society to maintain domestic legitimacy. Demonstrating the ability and willingness to disrupt these systems establishes deterrence in a way that targeted strikes against military communications nodes simply cannot.

Asymmetric Advantage and the Necessity of Preemptive Posture

The United States faces a fundamental strategic asymmetry in its approach to cyber warfare relative to its primary adversaries. American society is characterized by extraordinary connectivity, technological dependence, and infrastructure vulnerability—characteristics that make the nation simultaneously powerful and fragile. The American economy depends upon functioning power grids, financial networks, telecommunications systems, and transportation infrastructure in ways that create enormous potential vulnerability to cyber attack. Adversary nations, particularly authoritarian states with less developed technological infrastructures, are comparatively less dependent upon the specific systems that American cyber capabilities could target. This asymmetry means that in a pure cyber exchange, the United States has more to lose and less ability to impose equivalent costs through targeting similar systems.

The solution to this asymmetry lies not in pretending it does not exist but in leveraging the areas where American capabilities provide advantage. The United States possesses superior technological capabilities, deeper expertise in software and systems development, and greater resources devoted to cyber operations than any adversary nation. This advantage is most consequential when applied to the development of offensive capabilities specifically designed to target the critical infrastructure that adversary regimes depend upon for domestic stability and military function. By investing heavily in capabilities to cripple adversary power grids, financial systems, and communications networks, the United States creates a deterrent posture that addresses the asymmetry in vulnerability through an asymmetry in offensive capability. If adversaries recognize that attacking American infrastructure will trigger devastating attacks on their own civilian systems, the strategic calculus shifts dramatically in America's favor.

The preemptive dimension of this strategy deserves particular emphasis. Traditional deterrence theory focuses on retaliation following an attack—the threat of punishment designed to discourage aggression. Preemptive deterrence operates on a different logic, seeking to discourage attack by demonstrating that aggression will not achieve its objectives before those objectives can be realized. In the cyber domain, where attacks can occur in milliseconds and cause damage before defenders can respond, the distinction between preemptive and retaliatory action may be functionally meaningless. An adversary contemplating a cyber attack must believe not only that retaliation will eventually occur but that the attack itself may trigger immediate, devastating response. This perception can only be established through clear communication of doctrine, demonstrated capability through prior action, and maintained readiness to act decisively when American interests are threatened.

The Normative Argument: Reciprocity and International Order

Critics of offensive cyber operations against adversary critical infrastructure frequently invoke international law and the norms of armed conflict to argue that such actions would represent a dangerous departure from accepted practice. This argument fundamentally misunderstands both the legal framework governing cyber warfare and the practical requirements of maintaining international order in the digital age. International law does not prohibit the targeting of critical infrastructure during armed conflict; indeed, the ability to target enemy capacity to wage war represents a fundamental aspect of military doctrine that has been accepted since the emergence of modern nation-states. The question is not whether such targeting is categorically prohibited but under what circumstances it is permissible and what constraints should govern its execution.

The United States has been clear in its declared doctrine that it reserves the right to respond to cyber attacks with all appropriate means, including actions against adversary critical infrastructure. This doctrine, articulated in multiple presidential policy directives and military strategies, represents a legitimate exercise of the inherent right of self-defense recognized under international law. The violation of this doctrine by adversary nations—their ongoing attacks against American critical infrastructure in what amounts to a persistent, low-intensity cyber conflict—creates both the legal justification and moral necessity for response. To claim that American restraint in the face of such attacks represents adherence to international norms while adversary attacks represent mere violations of those same norms is to embrace a one-sided conception of international order that serves American interests poorly.

The deeper normative argument concerns the future of international order in the cyber domain. International norms are not fixed and eternal but are continuously negotiated through state practice, declaration, and response to provocation. When the United States and its allies fail to respond effectively to cyber attacks against critical infrastructure, they effectively normalize such attacks as acceptable behavior below the threshold of armed conflict. Adversary nations observe this pattern and adjust their behavior accordingly, escalating the frequency and sophistication of their operations. Conversely, when states demonstrate that attacks on critical infrastructure will trigger significant consequences—including analogous attacks on the aggressor's critical infrastructure—they establish a norm of reciprocity that may ultimately serve to constrain all parties. This norm may be uncomfortable, but it offers a realistic path to stability in a domain where existing norms have manifestly failed to protect American interests.

Escalation Management and Strategic Communication

The most serious objection to the strategy advocated here concerns the risk of escalation. Critics argue that attacking adversary critical infrastructure, even in response to prior attacks, risks triggering a spiral of escalation that could escalate to conventional military conflict or even nuclear exchange. This objection deserves serious consideration, as the avoidance of major power conflict represents perhaps the most important strategic objective for any American administration. However, the escalation objection rests on several assumptions that do not withstand scrutiny and, more importantly, ignores the escalatory risks inherent in the current American posture of restraint.

The first flawed assumption underlying the escalation objection is that adversaries are not already engaged in active cyber warfare against the United States. This assumption is simply false. American intelligence agencies have documented years of sophisticated cyber operations against American critical infrastructure by Russian, Chinese, Iranian, and North Korean actors. These operations have targeted power grids, water treatment facilities, financial systems, hospitals, and transportation networks. They have exfiltrated sensitive data, disrupted operations, and in some cases caused physical damage. The United States is not a passive victim contemplating whether to enter a cyber conflict; it is already engaged in a persistent cyber conflict in which it has been systematically outmatched in willingness to impose costs. The question is not whether to escalate but whether to continue accepting one-sided restraint or to establish a more sustainable equilibrium.

The second flawed assumption is that restraint reduces escalation risk while responsiveness increases it. This assumption inverts the actual dynamics of escalation in competitive domains. Adversaries test limits because they want to understand what actions will trigger response and what actions will be tolerated. When American responses to cyber attacks have been muted, delayed, or purely symbolic, adversaries have interpreted this as evidence that more aggressive actions remain below threshold for significant response. This interpretation encourages continued escalation as adversaries seek to determine the actual limits of American tolerance. Conversely, when adversaries have faced immediate, significant, and proportional responses to their cyber aggression, they have demonstrated remarkable capacity for restraint in subsequent operations. The historical record suggests that clear, consistent, and consequential response reduces escalation risk by establishing and communicating clear red lines.

Effective escalation management requires sophisticated strategic communication that clearly articulates the circumstances under which offensive cyber operations against adversary critical infrastructure will be authorized. This communication should occur through both public declarations and private diplomatic channels, ensuring that adversary leadership understands exactly what actions will trigger what responses. Such clarity serves to constrain adversary behavior by establishing predictable consequences while simultaneously providing adversaries with the information necessary to avoid inadvertent escalation. The current American approach, in which the boundaries of acceptable behavior remain ambiguous and responses are unpredictable in both timing and magnitude, creates maximum uncertainty and therefore maximum risk of miscalculation.

Implementation: Building the Capabilities and Will

The strategy advocated here requires substantial investment in capabilities that the United States currently lacks in sufficient quantity and sophistication. While American cyber operations have demonstrated remarkable technical capabilities in specific operations—Stuxnet representing perhaps the most famous example—the United States lacks the capacity to conduct sustained, large-scale cyber operations against adversary critical infrastructure comparable to the way the Air Force conducts air campaigns or the Navy conducts maritime operations. Closing this capability gap requires investment in several areas that deserve explicit attention.

First, the United States must develop a robust inventory of cyber weapons specifically designed to target the critical infrastructure systems used by adversary nations. This requires deep intelligence collection on the specific hardware and software controlling adversary power grids, financial systems, transportation networks, and communications infrastructure. It requires the development of exploits and payloads capable of reliably disrupting these systems while evading detection and countermeasures. It requires the establishment of redundant delivery mechanisms and the continuous testing and updating of weapons to ensure they remain effective as adversary systems evolve. This investment must be sustained over time, as cyber weapons have limited shelf lives as defenses improve and systems are updated.

Second, the United States must develop the organizational capacity to plan and execute large-scale cyber operations with the same rigor and professionalism that characterizes kinetic military operations. This requires dedicated units with trained personnel, established doctrine, realistic training environments, and clear command and control structures. It requires integration with broader military planning so that cyber operations can be synchronized with diplomatic messaging and kinetic force employment. The current model, in which cyber operations are conducted primarily by intelligence agencies with limited coordination and no unified command structure, cannot support the strategy advocated here.

Third, and perhaps most difficult, the United States must develop the political will to authorize and execute offensive cyber operations against adversary critical infrastructure when American interests demand it. This requires presidential leadership willing to accept the political and diplomatic costs of such actions. It requires congressional support for both the authorization of such operations and the protection of decision-makers from political attack when operations become public. It requires a media establishment capable of understanding and explaining the strategic necessity of offensive cyber operations rather than reflexively characterizing them as aggressive or illegal. Building this political will may be the most challenging aspect of implementing the strategy, but without it, all other investments will prove insufficient.

Conclusion: Accepting Responsibility for American Security

The United States cannot afford to remain passive in the face of ongoing cyber aggression from adversary nations. Every day that passes without significant response to attacks on American critical infrastructure establishes new precedents that disadvantage the United States and encourage continued adversary escalation. The development and deployment of offensive cyber capabilities targeting adversary critical infrastructure represents not an abandonment of American values but an assertion of the fundamental responsibility of government to protect its citizens from hostile action. This responsibility requires the capability and willingness to impose costs on those who attack the United States, and it requires the strategic doctrine to communicate clearly that such costs will be imposed predictably and consequentially.

The strategy outlined here is not without risk. Any significant military or quasi-military action carries the potential for escalation, miscalculation, and unintended consequences. But the absence of action carries risks as well—risks that have already materialized in the form of ongoing adversary cyber operations that have compromised American security, stolen American intellectual property, and threatened American lives. The choice is not between risk and safety but between different configurations of risk and reward. The current configuration systematically disadvantages the United States by allowing adversaries to attack with impunity while constraining American response. The alternative configuration—demonstrated capability, communicated willingness, and credible deterrence—offers the best available path toward a more stable and secure cyber environment.

The United States has historically led the development of international order, accepting the responsibilities that accompany great power status. In the cyber domain, this leadership requires the acceptance that the rules-based order will not defend itself. Adversary nations are actively working to undermine the stability and security that American leadership has provided, and they are doing so through means that existing international institutions and norms are unable to address. Meeting this challenge requires the United States to develop, demonstrate, and employ the capabilities necessary to defend American interests in the cyber domain, including the capability to strike adversary critical infrastructure when American security demands it. This is not an invitation to recklessness but an acceptance of the strategic necessity that defines great power competition in the twenty-first century. The security of the American people depends upon accepting this responsibility with the seriousness and commitment it demands.

Introduction

In an era where warfare increasingly transcends physical battlefields, the United States faces adversaries who operate aggressively in the digital domain. Nations like Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea have demonstrated both willingness and capability to target American critical infrastructure through cyberspace. The United States already faces persistent cyber aggression from numerous state actors. Russian operatives have penetrated U.S. electrical grids and election systems; Chinese state-sponsored hackers routinely target intellectual property and government networks; Iran has attempted disruptions against banking infrastructure; and North Korea has deployed destructive malware like WannaCry globally. These are not hypothetical scenarios but documented realities.

These adversaries are developing and deploying offensive cyber capabilities without hesitation. For example, Russia's 2015 and 2016 attacks on Ukraine's power grid demonstrated their willingness to weaponize cyber capabilities against critical infrastructure, plunging regions into darkness. The 2017 NotPetya attack—attributed to Russia—caused billions in damages globally. China's offensive cyber units operate with remarkable persistence and sophistication against Western targets. To maintain strategic parity, the United States cannot afford to cede this operational domain to adversaries.

The Strategic Case for Offensive Cyber Capabilities

Deterrence Through Demonstrated Capability

Effective deterrence requires credible capability and demonstrated willingness to use it. By developing and occasionally revealing offensive cyber capabilities against critical infrastructure targets, the United States can establish meaningful deterrence. When potential adversaries understand that attacks against American infrastructure could trigger devastating counter-strikes against their own power grids, financial systems, or other critical services, they must recalculate the cost-benefit analysis of launching cyber aggression.

Unlike nuclear deterrence, which relies on weapons that cannot be used without catastrophic consequences, cyber capabilities can be calibrated, demonstrated, and employed with precision. The United States can signal resolute determination by occasionally revealing capabilities or conducting limited operations that demonstrate potential consequences without triggering escalation to conventional conflict.

Preemption as a Necessary Option

In cyber warfare, the advantage frequently belongs to the first mover. Waiting to be attacked before responding can mean absorbing potentially catastrophic damage to critical national infrastructure. The ability to strike preemptively—disabling an adversary's offensive cyber capabilities or critical infrastructure before an imminent attack—represents a crucial strategic option.

When intelligence indicates an adversary is preparing cyber assault against American infrastructure, preemptive action may represent the only viable defense. For example, if credible intelligence revealed preparations for cyber attacks designed to disable the U.S. power grid during winter, preemptively neutralizing the adversary's capability could prevent American civilian casualties.

Cost-Effective Asymmetric Advantage

Offensive cyber capabilities offer a remarkably cost-effective means of projecting power and protecting national interests. Developing sophisticated cyber weapons requires significantly less investment than conventional military hardware while potentially delivering comparable strategic impact. For a fraction of the cost of an aircraft carrier battle group, the United States can develop cyber capabilities that could effectively deter aggression or respond to provocation without risking American lives.

This asymmetric advantage becomes particularly valuable against near-peer competitors with substantial conventional military resources. The ability to impose significant costs through cyber means creates strategic leverage that extends beyond the digital domain into broader geopolitical calculations.

Addressing Ethical and Legal Considerations

Proportionality and Discrimination

Critics rightfully raise concerns about attacking civilian infrastructure. However, a sophisticated offensive cyber program can incorporate principles of proportionality and discrimination from traditional warfare. Capabilities can be designed with precision, allowing temporary disruption rather than permanent destruction. For instance, systems that briefly disable power distribution networks but avoid damage to generation facilities could demonstrate resolve without causing humanitarian crises.

Additionally, the United States can develop capabilities that specifically target military command and control systems or dual-use infrastructure directly supporting adversary military operations. These approaches minimize civilian impact while maintaining deterrent value.

International Legal Framework

While critics argue that offensive cyber operations exist in a legal gray zone, the United States can help establish international norms by developing a transparent framework for their use. By articulating clear thresholds for deployment, demonstrating restraint, and advocating for international cyber agreements, America can shape responsible standards while maintaining necessary capabilities.

The United States has already taken steps in this direction through various policy documents, including the Department of Defense Cyber Strategy. Continuing to develop a clear doctrine around offensive cyber operations strengthens, rather than undermines, international stability by reducing uncertainty about American intentions and capabilities.

Implementation Considerations

Organizational Structure and Oversight

Developing offensive cyber capabilities requires robust institutional frameworks with appropriate civilian oversight. U.S. Cyber Command, working in coordination with the intelligence community and under direction from civilian leadership, provides this foundation. Congressional oversight committees can ensure operations remain aligned with American values and strategic objectives.

This structure allows for the integration of cyber capabilities with broader military and diplomatic strategies while maintaining democratic accountability. Rigorous civilian control ensures these capabilities serve defined national security objectives rather than expanding beyond necessary boundaries.

Clear Rules of Engagement

Effective deployment of offensive cyber capabilities requires explicit rules of engagement that define thresholds, approval chains, and operational parameters. These rules must balance operational flexibility with strategic discipline. For example, specified conditions might authorize limited defensive counter-cyber operations without requiring presidential approval, while major operations against critical infrastructure would demand highest-level authorization.

Such frameworks protect against unauthorized use while enabling timely response to emerging threats. They also provide clarity to adversaries about potential consequences of their actions against American interests.

Risk of Escalation

Critics frequently cite the danger of cyber operations escalating into conventional conflict. However, carefully calibrated offensive capabilities coupled with clear diplomatic messaging can actually reduce escalation risks. By establishing proportional response options below the threshold of kinetic warfare, the United States creates strategic off-ramps that might otherwise be absent.

Furthermore, failing to develop these capabilities could create more dangerous instability, where the only available responses to significant cyber aggression are either ineffectual diplomatic protests or dramatic conventional military responses.

Vulnerability to Retaliation

Opponents argue that America's own substantial digital vulnerability makes offensive operations too risky. This perspective fundamentally misunderstands deterrence dynamics. It is precisely because of American vulnerability that credible offensive capabilities are essential. Without them, adversaries can attack American infrastructure with minimal fear of meaningful consequences.

Rather than accepting vulnerability as a reason for restraint, the United States must simultaneously harden critical infrastructure while developing offensive capabilities that create mutually assured consequences in the cyber domain.

Conclusion

The digital battlefield is not a future theoretical concern but a present reality where adversaries already operate aggressively against American interests. Developing and maintaining offensive cyber capabilities against adversary critical infrastructure represents a strategic necessity, not a provocative option. Through careful implementation, robust oversight, and integration with broader national security strategy, such capabilities strengthen American security while potentially reducing the likelihood of both cyber and conventional conflicts.

America need not apologize for developing capabilities essential to protecting its citizens and interests. In a world where potential adversaries actively prepare to attack U.S. infrastructure, maintaining the capability to respond in kind represents responsible statecraft, not aggression. The United States must continue building these capabilities while leading international efforts to establish responsible norms for their use, creating a more stable global cyber environment through strength rather than unilateral restraint.

Deterrence in the Dark: The Case for a Declared American Offensive Cyber Doctrine

The next great war may not begin with missiles or invading armies. It may begin with darkness—hospitals losing power, financial networks freezing, water systems failing—before a single shot is fired. This is not speculation. America's principal adversaries have already decided that civilian critical infrastructure is a legitimate battlespace, and they have already placed themselves inside ours. The only serious question remaining is whether the United States will continue absorbing this quiet aggression under a posture of restraint that has purchased nothing, or whether it will do what great powers have always done to preserve peace: build a credible deterrent and declare the will to use it. The United States must develop, demonstrate, and publicly commit to the preemptive use of offensive cyber capabilities against the power grids and financial systems of adversary nations—not because war is desirable, but because deterrence in the twenty-first century is impossible without it.

The Threat Is Not Hypothetical

Consider the public record. In 2015 and 2016, hackers attributed to Russia's Sandworm unit seized control of Ukrainian power stations and plunged roughly a quarter-million people into darkness—the first confirmed cyber-induced blackouts in history. In 2017, the NotPetya malware, attributed to the same Russian military intelligence apparatus, escaped its intended targets and inflicted an estimated ten billion dollars in damage on global shipping, pharmaceutical, and logistics firms. Iran has been publicly tied to destructive attacks on Saudi Aramco, to years of denial-of-service campaigns against American banks, and to an intrusion into a dam control system in New York. North Korea, by U.S. and allied attribution, unleashed WannaCry and has systematically looted financial institutions to fund its weapons programs.

Most alarming is what U.S. officials have disclosed about Chinese state-sponsored actors—most notably the group known as Volt Typhoon—which American agencies have publicly described as burrowing into U.S. communications, energy, water, and transportation networks. Senior officials, including the FBI Director, testified to Congress that this activity was not espionage but pre-positioning: the placement of latent capabilities intended to disrupt American civilian life during a future crisis, such as a conflict over Taiwan, in order to sow panic and impede American military mobilization.

The conclusion is unavoidable. Adversary states have already crossed the threshold that American doctrine still treats as unthinkable. They operate with impunity because the costs we impose—indictments of unreachable hackers, sanctions of marginal bite, stern diplomatic statements—are trivial against the strategic value of holding American society hostage. Our restraint has not been reciprocated. It has been catalogued as weakness.

Defense Alone Is a Losing Strategy

Cyberspace is an offense-dominant domain. The defender must secure every device, every vendor, every software update, every employee click, forever. The attacker needs one gap, once. No amount of federal spending will make thousands of privately owned utilities, banks, and pipelines invulnerable, and the adversary knows it. A strategy of pure defense—"deterrence by denial"—asks Americans to accept that hostile implants will persist in their infrastructure indefinitely, activated at an enemy's leisure.

This is why every durable peace among great powers has rested not on defense alone but on deterrence by punishment: the credible threat that aggression will incur costs far exceeding any possible gain. As Thomas Schelling demonstrated in the nuclear age, deterrence is a psychological achievement. It requires capability and communicated will. Today the United States possesses formidable cyber capabilities but whispers about them, while its declaratory policy remains studiously ambiguous. An unstated deterrent deters no one.

The Logic of Preemption

Critics flinch at the word "preemptive." But they fail to grasp the temporal logic of cyber conflict. In the kinetic world, imminence can be measured in mobilized divisions and fueled aircraft. In cyberspace, the adversary's mobilization is the completed intrusion—the malware already sitting on grid control systems, awaiting a command. Once pre-positioning is discovered, the "attack" has, in every meaningful sense, already occurred; only the trigger pull remains. To wait for activation is to accept a first strike against American civilians as the price of responding.

A preemptive doctrine—striking or disabling adversary capabilities and the infrastructure that supports them before they can be used against us—is therefore not recklessness but anticipatory self-defense, a concept with deep roots in international law and American practice, from the Caroline standard to modern counterterrorism policy. Nor should the perishability of cyber access be ignored: network footholds are fleeting, patches close windows, and hesitation cedes the initiative permanently. A force designed to be used preemptively, under defined conditions and high-confidence attribution, is a force tailored to the actual physics of the domain. Anything slower is a force designed to lose.

Why Grids and Financial Systems Are the Right Targets

Holding adversary power grids and financial networks at risk is not only strategically sound; it is, paradoxically, the humane option. These systems constitute the modern center of gravity of every authoritarian state. Regimes in Moscow, Beijing, Tehran, and Pyongyang survive on economic function and domestic order; the prospect of both evaporating concentrates ruling minds far more effectively than threats to military hardware they rarely use.

Crucially, cyber effects against such targets can be made scalable, precise, and reversible in ways no bomb can match. A Tomahawk missile destroying a power station leaves rubble, dead engineers, and a decade of reconstruction. A cyber operation can darken that same grid for six hours and restore it with a keystroke—a demonstration of reach and restraint in a single act. Financial operations can corrupt settlement data, freeze payment networks, or drain regime accounts, imposing excruciating costs on elites without a single casualty. This is the ideal coercive instrument: severe enough to deter, calibrated enough to control, reversible enough to offer every party an off-ramp. A nation that possesses such options will resort to kinetic escalation less often, not more.

Declared Willingness Is the Deterrent Itself

Secret capabilities deter nothing; deterrence lives in the adversary's mind. The United States should therefore state plainly: any nation that pre-positions disruptive malware in American critical infrastructure, or conducts cyberattacks against it, accepts the certainty of American offensive action against its own power and financial systems—at a time of our choosing, preemptively if necessary, and without further warning.

Such clarity would transform the strategic landscape. Ambiguity invites probing; red lines discipline it. History teaches that miscalculation flourishes in the fog of unstated commitments, from 1914 to 1990. A declared doctrine, paired with demonstrated capability and standing presidential authorization for rapid employment, achieves escalation dominance: the adversary's knowledge that the United States can and will climb every rung of the ladder is precisely what keeps him off the first one. Existing policy—the "defend forward" and "persistent engagement" concepts in the 2018 Department of Defense Cyber Strategy, and the expanded authorities reported to have been granted to U.S. Cyber Command—already points in this direction. What remains is to close the credibility gap by saying, publicly and specifically, what the world already suspects.

The Counterarguments Fail

"It would violate international law." International humanitarian law prohibits indiscriminate attacks, not effective ones; dual-use infrastructure that supports military action has long been a lawful object of attack, and the right of self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter, including against imminent attack, is well established. Reversible cyber effects actually fare better under proportionality analysis than kinetic strikes. Moreover, norms are shaped by state practice. Unilateral American restraint does not build a legal order; it merely builds a target list. The path to genuine norms runs through enforcement—consequences that give rules meaning.

"We are the most vulnerable; retaliation would hurt us more." This confuses an argument for hardening with an argument against deterrence. We are being penetrated now, under restraint. Mutual vulnerability did not cause nuclear war; it helped prevent one, by making aggression irrational. The answer to our exposure is resilience plus credible threat—not hope masquerading as strategy.

"It risks uncontrolled escalation." Escalation is likelier when adversaries misjudge our resolve than when they are certain of it. Cyber tools, uniquely, offer reversible, deniable, graduated rungs—off-ramps that missiles do not. Clear doctrine reduces the ambiguity in which wars begin.

"Attribution is too uncertain." American attribution capabilities have matured dramatically, as repeated public attributions and detailed indictments show. A serious doctrine can demand high-confidence attribution and presidential authorization—standards entirely compatible with decisive action.

"It erodes America's moral standing." There is no moral majesty in permitting adversaries to believe they can switch off American hospitals at negligible cost. The norm against attacking civilian infrastructure cannot survive if only democracies observe it. Norms without enforcement are fictions; strength precedes law.

The Moral Case for Strength

The ultimate argument is humanitarian. The nuclear deterrent's greatest triumph is that it was never used in anger after 1945: great-power war, the scourge of the preceding thirty years, receded because the consequences became unthinkable. A cyber deterrent that never has to fire would be an equally profound humanitarian achievement. And preemption can be the very thing that prevents wars: an adversary who knows his grid will go dark and his banks will freeze before his first missile launches has the strongest possible incentive to keep that missile in its silo.

The choice before the United States is not between a world with cyber conflict and one without it. That world arrived while we were being polite. The choice is between a declared deterrent that keeps the lights on, and a posture of vulnerable restraint that invites the darkness in. America should develop these capabilities without apology, demonstrate them without ambiguity, and declare its willingness to use them—preemptively, proportionately, and with resolve. Peace through strength was right in the industrial age. It is indispensable in the digital one.

Strength Through Restraint: The Case for a Responsible U.S. Offensive Cyber Capability

The United States should develop and maintain formidable offensive cyber capabilities. In an era when hostile governments can disrupt communications, steal military secrets, sabotage industry, and threaten essential services without crossing a physical border, relying on defensive measures alone would leave the nation dangerously exposed. A credible capacity to impose costs in cyberspace can deter aggression, provide alternatives to conventional warfare, and help the United States respond rapidly to imminent threats. Yet this capability must be governed by a crucial distinction: possessing powerful cyber weapons is prudent; embracing preemptive attacks on civilian power grids and financial systems is not.

Cyber deterrence requires more than firewalls and warnings. Adversaries are less likely to launch major attacks if they believe the United States can identify those responsible and respond against assets their governments value. Accordingly, U.S. Cyber Command and intelligence agencies should be able to disrupt hostile military networks, disable infrastructure directly supporting an imminent attack, dismantle state-sponsored cyber operations, and neutralize servers used for espionage, ransomware, or destructive activity. Such options may prevent conflict by demonstrating that cyber aggression will carry tangible consequences.

Offensive cyber tools can also provide a more proportionate alternative to bombs and missiles. If a hostile military is preparing an attack, temporarily disabling its command network may be less destructive than striking its headquarters. If malware is poised to damage American infrastructure, deleting it or severing the attacker’s access may avert casualties without requiring conventional force. Properly designed cyber operations can therefore expand the range of choices available to national leaders and reduce pressure to escalate immediately to kinetic warfare.

Nevertheless, civilian critical infrastructure should not become a routine instrument of coercion. Power grids sustain hospitals, emergency communications, water treatment, food storage, transportation, and heating. Financial systems distribute wages, pensions, and disaster assistance. Crippling them can rapidly endanger people who have no meaningful connection to their government’s actions. Malware may also spread beyond its intended target, remain hidden after a crisis ends, or be copied and reused by criminals and rival states.

Preemptive attacks on such systems could weaken rather than strengthen American security. The United States is among the world’s most digitally dependent societies, giving it an enormous stake in preserving norms against attacks on civilian infrastructure. If Washington openly treats foreign grids and banks as acceptable first-strike targets, adversaries will cite that precedent when targeting American utilities, hospitals, and markets. An aggressive doctrine may invite cyber arms racing, encourage states to launch attacks before losing access, and turn an uncertain warning into a self-fulfilling conflict.

A more credible doctrine would combine strength with strict limits. The United States should maintain access and capabilities sufficient to respond to major cyber aggression, but authorize operations according to necessity, proportionality, distinction, and careful assessment of foreseeable civilian effects. Preemptive action should require compelling evidence of an imminent threat and should focus first on the hostile operation itself: its malware, command servers, military communications, launch infrastructure, and responsible units. Operations against dual-use or civilian systems should face the highest level of review and occur only when lawful, genuinely necessary to prevent grave harm, and designed to minimize duration, spillover, and humanitarian consequences.

This doctrine should be reinforced through congressional oversight, executive review, legal scrutiny, allied consultation where feasible, and rigorous technical testing. Decision-makers should require plans for reversibility, containment, incident response, and post-operation remediation. The government should also strengthen attribution capabilities and communicate privately or publicly, as circumstances permit, which conduct will trigger a response. Deterrence is most effective when adversaries understand both American capabilities and the boundaries governing their use.

Finally, offensive capacity cannot substitute for resilience. Secure software, segmented networks, backup power, rapid recovery plans, public-private coordination, and protection of election, health, energy, and financial systems remain indispensable. Securing America's Future: The Strategic Imperative for Offensive Cyber Capabilities

In an era where ones and zeros can inflict as much damage as bombs and bullets, the United States faces a critical decision about its national security posture. As nation-states increasingly weaponize cyberspace, America must develop and maintain robust offensive cyber warfare capabilities targeting adversaries' critical infrastructure. While this proposition may seem aggressive, it represents a necessary evolution in deterrence strategy that could paradoxically prevent conflicts and save lives by making the costs of aggression prohibitively high for potential adversaries.

The New Battlefield: Why Traditional Defenses Are Insufficient

The digital transformation of modern society has created unprecedented vulnerabilities. Power grids, financial systems, water treatment facilities, and transportation networks all depend on interconnected computer systems. While the United States has invested heavily in cyber defense, a purely defensive posture is fundamentally flawed. As any security expert will attest, determined attackers with sufficient resources will eventually find vulnerabilities. The asymmetric nature of cyber warfare—where attacks are cheap but defense is expensive—means that adversaries can probe American defenses indefinitely until they succeed.

Consider recent history: the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack in 2021 disrupted fuel supplies across the Eastern United States, while the SolarWinds breach compromised thousands of government and private systems. These incidents, perpetrated by criminal groups and nation-states respectively, demonstrate that defensive measures alone cannot guarantee security. The United States needs the capability to impose costs on adversaries who contemplate such attacks.

Deterrence in the Digital Age

The concept of deterrence has successfully prevented major power conflicts since World War II. Nuclear weapons created a balance of terror that made large-scale warfare between superpowers unthinkable. Offensive cyber capabilities can serve a similar deterrent function in the 21st century. When adversaries know that attacks on American infrastructure will trigger devastating retaliation against their own critical systems, they must carefully weigh the costs and benefits of aggression.

This deterrent effect only works if capabilities are credible and adversaries believe the United States possesses both the ability and willingness to use them. Just as nuclear deterrence requires demonstrated capability and declared doctrine, cyber deterrence demands that potential adversaries understand the consequences of crossing red lines. The ability to preemptively disrupt an adversary's infrastructure before they can launch attacks adds another layer to this deterrent framework.

Strategic Advantages of Offensive Capabilities

Offensive cyber weapons offer unique strategic advantages that complement traditional military capabilities:

Precision and Proportionality: Unlike kinetic weapons, cyber tools can target specific systems with surgical precision. Disrupting a particular military command network or financial system can achieve strategic objectives without broader destruction or loss of life.

Reversibility: Many cyber effects can be temporary and reversible. Power grids can be restored, financial systems can be brought back online. This allows for flexible response options that can escalate or de-escalate as situations demand.

Cost-Effectiveness: Developing cyber capabilities requires far less resources than traditional weapons systems. A team of skilled programmers can create tools that achieve strategic effects comparable to billion-dollar weapons platforms.

Plausible Deniability: While attribution in cyberspace is improving, it remains challenging. This ambiguity can provide decision-makers with options below the threshold of traditional warfare.

Addressing Ethical and Practical Concerns

Critics rightfully raise concerns about targeting civilian infrastructure and the potential for escalation. These concerns must be addressed through careful policy development:

Strict Protocols: Offensive cyber operations should be subject to rigorous oversight, similar to nuclear weapons. Clear chains of command, legal review, and proportionality assessments must govern their use.

Discrimination in Targeting: Capabilities should be designed to minimize civilian harm. Temporary disruption of financial systems that pressure governments differs fundamentally from attacks on hospitals or water treatment facilities that directly harm civilians.

International Norms: The United States should lead efforts to establish international norms around cyber warfare, similar to the Geneva Conventions. However, until such agreements exist and are verifiable, unilateral restraint only disadvantages America.

Escalation Management: Clear doctrine must outline how cyber operations fit within broader escalation ladders. Decision-makers need frameworks for preventing cyber conflicts from spiraling into kinetic warfare.

The Cost of Inaction

The alternative to developing offensive capabilities is not a peaceful cyber domain—it is a domain where America's adversaries operate with impunity. China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea have all demonstrated willingness to target American infrastructure and steal intellectual property. Without credible deterrence, these attacks will intensify.

Moreover, in future conflicts, adversaries will certainly target American infrastructure. Would it not be preferable to disable an adversary's command and control systems through cyber means rather than conventional bombing? Is temporarily disrupting a power grid not more humane than a traditional military campaign?

Conclusion: A Necessary Evolution

The development of offensive cyber capabilities represents not militarism but realism. In a world where critical infrastructure depends on vulnerable computer networks, where adversaries actively develop and deploy cyber weapons, and where traditional defenses prove insufficient, the United States must adapt its security posture.

This adaptation requires careful consideration of ethical implications, robust oversight mechanisms, and clear strategic doctrine. But the fundamental logic remains sound: in cyberspace as in other domains, the best defense requires a credible offense. American security in the 21st century depends on recognizing this reality and acting accordingly.

The choice is not between a militarized or peaceful cyberspace—that choice has already been made by America's adversaries. The choice is whether the United States will possess the tools necessary to defend its interests and deter aggression in this new domain. For the sake of national security and global stability, America must choose strength.

  • Military communications jamming affects only enemy forces, not civilian internet users.

The United States can no longer afford a passive, reactive approach to cyber warfare. Adversaries like Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea are actively developing and deploying offensive cyber capabilities, and the U.S. must match this aggression with a credible deterrent.

Failure to act now will mean paying a far higher price later.
